planting.note: Frost-seed onto bare or thawing ground in late winter, or drill in early spring as soon as soil can be worked; Hubam is the true annual selection of white sweetclover, completing its life cycle and blooming in a single season rather than requiring a second year like standard biennial white and yellow sweetclover.

directions: Scarify or inoculate seed with the appropriate Rhizobium strain before broadcasting at 10-15 lb/acre onto a firm seedbed, since Hubam establishes best with good seed-to-soil contact but shallow coverage. Unlike its biennial sweetclover relatives, Hubam flowers and sets seed in its first year, making it useful where a quick nitrogen-fixing summer cover or bee-forage planting is needed without carrying a stand into a second season. Growth is rapid and upright once established, tolerating poor, droughty, or alkaline soils that discourage many other cover legumes. Mow or incorporate at early bloom for maximum nitrogen contribution, and allow several weeks before planting a following crop since the foliage carries the same coumarin compounds found in other sweetclovers.
sources: SARE (Sustainable Agriculture Research and Education) — Managing Cover Crops Profitably

common_name: Huia White Clover (New Zealand-Bred Grazing and Cover Crop White Clover)

planting.note: Sow in fall or early spring onto a firm, moist seedbed; Huia is the classic medium-leaved white clover cultivar bred in New Zealand and used worldwide as the reference standard against which newer white clover releases are measured.

directions: Broadcast fine seed onto a firm, weed-free seedbed in fall or early spring and roll or rake lightly, since Huia establishes poorly if buried deep. Bred in New Zealand from elite parent plants selected for balanced summer and winter growth, dense habit, and disease resistance, it combines medium-sized leaves with vigorous stolon spread to form a dense, persistent nitrogen-fixing groundcover. Its balanced season-long growth makes it a dependable choice for orchard alleys, pasture renovation, and living-mulch plantings across a wide range of temperate climates. Mow periodically to encourage stolon branching and keep the stand dense and weed-suppressive.
sources: New Zealand Journal of Agricultural Research

common_name: Madrid Yellow Sweetclover (Drought-Tolerant High-Vigor Yellow Sweetclover)

planting.note: Direct-sow in early spring or late summer on well-drained, calcareous, or dry soils; Madrid was selected in the southwestern United States for stronger seedling vigor, better fall-freeze survival, and greater drought tolerance than common yellow sweetclover strains.

directions: Scarify hard-coated seed and inoculate with the correct Rhizobium strain before broadcasting at 10-12 lb/acre, pressing seed lightly into a firm bed. Madrid was bred for improved seedling vigor and biomass production over common yellow sweetclover, along with noticeably better survival through early fall freezes and stronger performance on thin, dry, calcareous soils where many other legumes struggle. Like other yellow sweetclovers it forms a rosette in its first year, overwinters, then bolts and blooms in its second spring; terminate at early bud stage for maximum nitrogen return. Give incorporated residue three to four weeks to break down before planting a following crop, since coumarin in the foliage can temporarily suppress germination.
sources: New Mexico State University Cooperative Extension

common_name: Nitro Persian Clover (Prostrate Early-Maturing Persian Clover)

planting.note: Broadcast in late summer or early fall in moist, well-drained soil; Nitro is a prostrate, fine-stemmed Persian clover cultivar that matures earlier and sets more hard seed than the taller, broad-leaved majus-type Persian clovers.

directions: Broadcast seed onto a firm, moist seedbed in late summer or early fall and rake lightly for good seed-to-soil contact. Nitro belongs to the low-growing resupinatum type of Persian clover, distinguished from taller majus-type strains by its thinner stems, smaller leaflets, and more prostrate spreading habit, along with earlier flowering and higher hard-seed content that favors reliable volunteer reseeding. Its dense, mat-forming growth tolerates close mowing and light traffic better than upright clovers, making it useful as a low winter living mulch as well as a conventional nitrogen-fixing cover crop. Mow or incorporate at early flowering if reseeding is not wanted, or let a final flush bloom for early-season pollinator forage.
sources: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service — Plant Fact Sheets

common_name: Balady Berseem Clover (Traditional Single-Cut Egyptian Clover)

planting.note: Sow in late summer to early fall in warm-winter regions; Balady is the traditional high-growing-point, single-cut berseem clover landrace long grown in the Nile Delta, less cold-hardy than modern multi-cut cultivars like Frosty or Joe Burton.

directions: Broadcast inoculated seed onto a fine, fertile seedbed in late summer or early fall and rake lightly for even coverage. Balady is the traditional single-cut berseem type with a high growing point, growing quickly upright and moving to flower and seed on a narrower harvest window than modern multi-cut cultivars, so it recovers poorly if cut or grazed too early. It winterkills more readily than cold-bred selections like Frosty, making it best suited to mild-winter regions where a single heavy flush of biomass ahead of spring planting is the goal rather than repeated cuttings. Terminate by mowing and incorporating at early bloom for the greatest nitrogen contribution to a following crop.
sources: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service — Plant Guide (Berseem Clover, TRAL6)
SARE (Sustainable Agriculture Research and Education) — Berseem Clover

planting.note: Broadcast onto a firm seedbed in early fall; Clare belongs to the brachycalycinum subspecies of subterranean clover, distinct from Dalkeith, Mt. Barker, Nangeela, and Woogenellup, and is notably more tolerant of neutral to alkaline soils.

directions: Broadcast seed over a firm, moist bed in early fall and rake lightly, since reliable establishment depends on shallow, even seed placement. Clare stands apart from the more common subterraneum-type subclovers by belonging to the brachycalycinum subspecies, giving it markedly better tolerance of neutral to alkaline soils where other subterranean clovers thin out, along with vigorous seedling growth and robust regrowth when mowed regularly. Like other subclovers it buries its own seed pods just below the soil surface after flowering, allowing self-reseeding stands to persist for years with no replanting. Use it as a low, reseeding living mulch under fruit trees or in orchard alleys on higher-pH ground where Mt. Barker or Dalkeith would otherwise struggle.
sources: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service — Plant Fact Sheets
